Appendix I hERG assay allocation experiments

I.1 Model, data and execution

The model and execution settings were fixed across conditions (Table I1); prediction calibration and the selection and triage rules were fixed before capture. Internal evaluation on 2,009 held-out compounds achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.814; the healthy Top-402 contained 351 compounds labeled as blockers in the benchmark (87.31%) at about 20% of the pool. A pass computes the cohort with all three members; a source is one saved pass under one condition, and a technical block groups captures with their matched references. Molecular graphs and input order are preserved. Selection ranks calibrated probabilities with lexical identifier ties; triage assigns compounds to patch-clamp testing at or above the fixed threshold and to advancement without testing otherwise.

The retrospective series used two technical blocks with four repeats per condition, the first primary. Native Biomni cohorts covered selection, triage and 51 trajectories used to evaluate restoration budgets without rerunning the predictor. Confirmation used eight balanced blocks, each with a pass under each Case, BF16 matched references on the hardware that produced the faulty passes before and after its two Case passes, and a healthy reference obtained with the same GPU model on the same host. The eight healthy reference states and 16 matched reference states had identical saved predictions and linear-layer inputs and outputs. Biomni’s execution graph was unchanged, and the agent received neither expected decisions nor fault locations. The single-request experiment reused the 16 confirmation fault sources and one shared healthy reference without new captures; trusted recomputation on a healthy data-center GPU reproduced that reference bit for bit (Appendix I.7).

I.2 Object-level agent decisions

Decisions in this subsection are outputs of native Biomni trajectories in the confirmation series. Each combination of source and task had three repeats with identical primary decisions, and all 36 Case 2 trajectories whose inputs changed a decision applied the stated rule to their input. Probabilities are calibrated ensemble means, the reference is the healthy BF16 state from the same host, and the triage threshold is given in Table I1.

All six exchanged compounds carry blocker labels. Except for K8429, healthy ranks were 397–406, within 0.0039 of the selection boundary. K12096 and K2422 entered with unchanged predictions when competitors fell; their shared probability 0.794193 gave K12096 the single vacancy in block 8 by lexical order. K8429 fell from rank 211 to 821 in block 7, with ensemble standard deviation rising from 0.0194 to 0.4165, above the reference maximum 0.3517.

Against 1,407 reference decisions to assign patch-clamp testing, Case 2 produced six removals and six additions. Removals included blockers K12252 and K1461; the other changes concerned compounds labeled as non-blockers in the benchmark. K13418 and K13388 were closest to the healthy threshold, with adjacent attainable calibrated probabilities about 0.0003 apart. R1 restored eleven of twelve changes; R1+M recovered the remaining K13418 assay in block 3 (R1 residual 0.000629). R1 also restored the Case 1 block 4 change to K13418.

Boundary or tie tables appeared in 30/36 trajectories whose inputs changed a decision; 24 listed an affected compound (Table I5). K8429, displaced to rank 821, appeared in none. K4780 appeared in all three tables for block 7 at margin 0.0015, and none of the six tables for blocks 1 and 5 at margins 0.017 and 0.031. A report for block 6 advanced K13388 at margin −0.000041-0.000041, versus its healthy +0.000273+0.000273. Named compounds were boundary or near-threshold cases. All 36 reports stated that the inputs were finite; 18 reported reproducing the calibration within 1.67×10−161.67\times 10^{-16}. No output used ensemble disagreement as a decision criterion, called the predictor or referred to hardware faults.

In the 16 retrospective BF16 sources, decisions implied by the inputs changed for eight of the twelve confirmation compounds: K5612, K8400, K12096, K5629 and K2422 in selection, and K13388, K4780 and K13418 in triage. K13388 was assigned to advancement without testing in six retrospective sources, and K5612 left the list in three. The faults moved compounds at healthy margins from 0.00004 to 0.085, so the affected set is defined jointly by the decision boundaries and by where the faulty arithmetic displaces values.

I.3 Retrospective coordinate budgets and biochemical anchors

Continuation resumed at the output of the second feed-forward layer, before the final activation and output layer. All reference and candidate member predictions replayed bit for bit in three BF16 passes. The editable target scope was 3×3003\times 300 coordinates, against 1,808,100 for the cohort; every integer prefix of each prespecified coordinate order was tested.

Matches of the complete InChIKey against ChEMBL 35 link K5612 to CHEMBL3804918 (radioligand displacement, IC50 434 ±\pm 29 nM, Ki 217 nM) and K7714 to CHEMBL2207660 (radioligand displacement, IC50 1,995 nM) [55, 56]. In the retrospective BF16 selection tasks, K5612 fell from rank 397 to 415 or 421, and matching restoration returned it to the list. In the retrospective triage task, K7714 was assigned to advancement without testing while the number assigned to testing remained 1,407.

Coordinates were ordered before scanning by their mean absolute difference across eight earlier development passes, with ties broken by index; a co-occurrence order and three random orders were retained, and biological labels did not determine priority. Strict locality required each touched member row to retain differences and the visible prediction vector to differ from the destination. The numbers of differing coordinates were 291, 567 and 850 in the target rows, and 135,225, 138,222 and 134,646 across the cohort.

The three restored decisions coexisted with 303, 317 and 276 calibrated cohort predictions still differing from the reference, respectively. Each touched member row retained differences under the strict locality rule.

With the co-occurrence order and three random orders, first successful prefixes ranged from 64 to 458 restored and 24 to 160 transplanted coordinates for K5612, and from 1 to 40 restored and 635 to 846 transplanted coordinates for K7714. Reference inputs restored the full decisions. The 22 conditions contained 17 distinct inputs, each evaluated in three trajectories (51 total).

I.4 Arithmetic verification and timing

The audit covered eight BF16 passes per Case and eight each for reference computation on the same device and restoration. Removing duplicate calculations with the same ensemble member, layer, operands and outputs left 5,232 linear calculations. For Y=X​W⊤+bY=XW^{\top}+b, BF16-quantized operands gave FP64 expected row and column sums on a healthy GPU, with allowances for accumulation, intermediate and final rounding. Scope and thresholds were fixed before audit; an independent CPU implementation agreed on all calculations. Checksums localized 695 of 991 Case 1 observations with errors identified by elementwise checks and all 2,256 Case 2 observations. The 16 reference and restoration passes were unflagged, with no false alarm in eight healthy verifier runs.

Per Case, integrity checks on stored data and checks that final probabilities were finite and between 0 and 1 each flagged 0/8 passes; row and column checksums with a fixed rounding bound and elementwise arithmetic recomputation each flagged 8/8.

In the confirmation series, recomputing the R1 units with the original batch geometry retained the K13418 triage discrepancy, and restoration with reference values recovered every member prediction in all eight Case 2 sources.

The confirmation R1 medians were 0.2164–0.3197 s for 2,168–3,283 recomputed predictions from individual ensemble members per Case 2 source. The margin step took a median of 0.0333 s, including selection, graph repacking, transfer to the GPU, inference and writeback. Timings exclude model loading, graph construction, cross-machine transfer and archival.

The streaming implementation shares signed and absolute FP64 tile reductions for row and column checks. A conservative arithmetic guard determines the original FP64 check’s flag decision when rounding bounds leave it unambiguous, and otherwise invokes that check. Across the 16 fault sources, flags and localization matched the original checks, and R1 and R1+M arrays were bitwise identical. Relative to the original FP64 implementation, streaming reduced the verified forward time by 42.4% and the added verification time by 78.2%; its overhead relative to the native forward path was 25.8%.

I.5 Adding a margin rule to R1

Development used the 16 retrospective R1 sources. The threshold ε\varepsilon was twice their largest absolute calibrated residual relative to the healthy reference (Table I1); it was fixed before evaluation on the 16 confirmation sources. The rule uses only current R1 probabilities p^i\hat{p}_{i}. The triage margin is |p^i−t||\hat{p}_{i}-t|. With compounds sorted by decreasing probability and lexical ties, the selection margin is p^i−p^(403)\hat{p}_{i}-\hat{p}_{(403)} for selected compounds and p^(402)−p^i\hat{p}_{(402)}-\hat{p}_{i} otherwise. The union of compounds with either margin strictly below ε\varepsilon was recomputed once, all three members, in original order and in batches of at most 128, while unselected predictions remained unchanged. Reference predictions and labels were inaccessible during recomputation.

The rule selected 68 compounds, 39 through the triage margin and 29 through the ranking margin, with no overlap, and the same 68 in every source evaluated. Multipliers 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 of ε\varepsilon selected 0, 16, 34, 68, 146 and 306 compounds; triage agreement was 15/16 at multiplier 0 and 16/16 at every nonzero multiplier, and multiplier 1 remained the primary policy. Residuals that changed decisions were small, 0.000629 for K13388 in a retrospective Case 1 source and 0.000629 for K13418, whereas a residual of 0.0311 for K4999, whose healthy probability is 0.6468, changed neither decision; its R1 score remained 0.18 from the nearer boundary. The five confirmation residuals larger than the largest retrospective residual, two of them also larger than ε\varepsilon (0.0311 for K4999 and 0.0111 for K8408), all lay at least 0.064 from the nearer boundary after R1 and changed no decision. Six benign BF16 settings on healthy hardware, each repeated eight times, reproduced the BF16 predictions and decisions bit for bit.

I.6 Native agent continuation

The three triage outputs on the original inputs for Case 1 block 4 consistently added K13418, giving 1,408 decisions to assign patch-clamp testing against 1,407 in the reference, and the R1 outputs recovered the reference action. All 38 combinations of source and task had three valid trajectories with identical primary decisions, and all 19 selection groups also had identical order within the list. The R1 and R1+M inputs for block 4 were identical but kept separate planned repeats, so the 19 conditions represent 18 distinct prediction tables. No trajectory called the prediction service.

I.7 Recovery and commitment for each request

Each request is defined by one source, task and repeat: the 16 confirmation fault sources and one shared healthy reference, two tasks and three repeats give 102 requests. The 39 changed decisions came from 13 combinations of source and task, each repeated three times. Each request was evaluated separately under three recovery conditions: recovery before the agent read the predictions, file replacement after it had read them, and restoration of the execution state saved before that read. The two later conditions shared one executed prefix in which native Biomni read the prediction table, wrote its report and prepared an action. File replacement corrected the prediction file while retaining visible history, Python variables, derived files and pending actions. State restoration returned to the checkpoint before the first read, restored files and the Python environment, discarded dependent state and pending actions, and continued with the certified table. Prompts and tools were unchanged, and no prompt mentioned faults or recomputation.

Every condition obtained a certificate from full trusted recomputation, including runs without an arithmetic flag. Each condition had a separate local commit record, so the limit of one commitment per request applied within each condition. In one transaction, it checked the request, certificate, computation contract, input view, agreement with the certified decision and prior commitment; it recorded accepted actions without changing the agent’s proposal. Commitment was a local record of an accepted assay allocation. When only the prediction file was replaced, all 96 actions on fault inputs were rejected because the input view used to prepare them had been superseded, including 57 that agreed with the healthy decision. The six accepted actions were healthy controls (Table I10).

On the saved arrays, R1 recovered both decisions in all 16 sources except one triage vector (Case 2, block 3), and R1+M in all 16, while 5–16 and 4–15 of 6,027 member predictions, respectively, still differed. Full trusted recomputation eliminated the remaining differences; all 306 certified computations produced the same prediction array.

Raw predictions and saved tensors were finite, and the captures raised no warning. All 102 prefixes applied the rule to their own input, and the three repeats of each combination of source and task made the same decision. No trajectory called the prediction service, and no report identified a numerical fault.

Appendix J Screening experiments

J.1 27B agents on new screening inputs

The schedule fixed 48 ESOL molecular and 48 CITE-seq cell operations before fresh capture [41, 58]. CD3 and CD14 yield 144 contexts, each run under 14 conditions, including repeated reference and fault states and complete reference replay: 2,016 serial Qwen3.8-27B trajectories. Repeated reference and repeated Case 2 states agreed within condition on queried objects, their order and hit count. Measurements were unavailable until queried; the predictor was not refitted (Table J1).

Case 2 changed the shortlist in 62 contexts, the objects chosen for measurement in 38 and the number of measurements meeting the task threshold in 11. Every report matched returned measurements; rerunning the agent on reference values recovered all 38 changed choices.

Case 2 changed a median of 71.5 coordinates per ESOL operation and 199 per CITE-seq operation, with median maximum displacements of 0.24 and 0.33. For the tool’s 24-item shortlist, let di=|μi−t|d_{i}=|\mu_{i}-t| for reference means μi\mu_{i} and fixed threshold tt. Sort dd increasingly and set g=d(25)−d(24)g=d_{(25)}-d_{(24)}. If e=maxi⁡|μ^i−μi|e=\max_{i}|\widehat{\mu}_{i}-\mu_{i}|, then ||μ^i−t|−di|≤e\big||\widehat{\mu}_{i}-t|-d_{i}\big|\leq e; hence g>2​eg>2e certifies unchanged membership (Appendix C.4). Of the 144 Case 2 comparisons, this sufficient condition certified 16 ESOL shortlists, all unchanged; the shortlist changed in 62.

All 40 Case 2 context pairs with a repeated behavioral difference, 38 changes in the objects chosen for measurement and two changes in secondary endpoints, entered a factorial comparison of list membership and numerical values. Each condition combined reference or candidate list membership with the reference or candidate numerical fields of the same identifiers, with four repetitions per pair (Table J3). In mixed displays, choices did not follow the source of the list alone: reference lists with candidate values matched the reference query set in 84 of 160 trajectories, and candidate lists with reference values in 32 of 160. Both which objects are listed and the values attached to them steer the agent’s choices.

J.2 Screening cells from held-out donors

Donors P7 and P8 were absent from earlier captured rows, the labeled fitting set and landmarks. Existing transformations, predictor and thresholds were retained. Two technical blocks ran in opposite Case order, each with four captures under matched reference, Case 1, Case 2 and fresh recovery; first captures were prespecified as primary. The independent CPU check used represented BF16 operands and bounds for FP32 accumulation and final BF16 rounding; it took 0.061 s, with array comparisons taking 4.7–6.0 ms. All 32 captures completed with finite outputs and raised no warning or exception. Each Case 2 capture had 116–127 coordinates whose errors exceeded the numerical bounds; fresh reference computation recovered both changed primary CD3 classifications per block. Case 1 and CD14 had no changed primary classification.

Appendix K Certified commitment

K.1 Contract, admissible sets and Proposition 1

Fix inputs, model, representation, execution settings, candidate set and tie rule, defining reference scores p⋆∈ℝnp^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and decision map g:ℝn→𝒜g:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathcal{A}. The hERG contract is healthy BF16 computation (Table I1). Trusted recomputation fixes a score only when it reproduces its reference exactly, using the original geometry or regrouped batches when the arithmetic for each item is independent of batch size and composition. Recomputed hERG scores matched their references bit for bit in the tested sources (Section 5.2). Other values enter through valid bounds. At round rr, current scores are s(r)s^{(r)} and FrF_{r} indexes fixed scores. Assume validity, p⋆∈𝒰rp^{\star}\in\mathcal{U}_{r}, and persistence, Fr⊆Fr+1F_{r}\subseteq F_{r+1} with qi=pi⋆q_{i}=p^{\star}_{i} for all q∈𝒰rq\in\mathcal{U}_{r}, i∈Fri\in F_{r}.

Correctness. If g⁡(q)=ag(q)=a for every q∈𝒰rq\in\mathcal{U}_{r}, validity gives g⁡(p⋆)=ag(p^{\star})=a, so a committed decision equals the reference decision.

Termination. Suppose every round that ends without certification adds at least one index to FrF_{r}. If no earlier round certifies, then Fn={1,…,n}F_{n}=\{1,\ldots,n\}; persistence gives 𝒰n⊆{p⋆}\mathcal{U}_{n}\subseteq\{p^{\star}\}, validity gives 𝒰n={p⋆}\mathcal{U}_{n}=\{p^{\star}\}, and gg is constant on 𝒰n\mathcal{U}_{n}. Certification is therefore reached within nn rounds.

Certification concerns agreement with the reference computation; Algorithm 3 handles agent and service failures.

K.2 Interval evidence, thresholds and Top-K sets

Let ss be the current scores with valid bounds |si−pi⋆|≤ei|s_{i}-p^{\star}_{i}|\leq e_{i}, where ei=0e_{i}=0 for i∈Fri\in F_{r}. The admissible set is the box 𝒰={q:|qi−si|≤ei​for all​i}\mathcal{U}=\{q:|q_{i}-s_{i}|\leq e_{i}\ \text{for all}\ i\}, which contains p⋆p^{\star}.

Corollary 1 (interval evidence). Let |si−pi⋆|≤ei|s_{i}-p^{\star}_{i}|\leq e_{i} for the current scores ss, with ei=0e_{i}=0 for recomputed scores. For the rule qi≥tq_{i}\geq t, the decision for item ii is certified when si−ei≥ts_{i}-e_{i}\geq t or si+ei<ts_{i}+e_{i}<t. A Top-KK set SS is certified when si−ei>sj+ejs_{i}-e_{i}>s_{j}+e_{j} for every i∈Si\in S and j∉Sj\notin S.

Proof.

Threshold. For the rule qi≥tq_{i}\geq t, if si−ei≥ts_{i}-e_{i}\geq t then qi≥tq_{i}\geq t for every q∈𝒰q\in\mathcal{U}, and if si+ei<ts_{i}+e_{i}<t then qi<tq_{i}<t. The decision for item ii is therefore constant on 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

Top-K. For observed Top-KK set SS, the interval condition gives qi≥si−ei>sj+ej≥qjq_{i}\geq s_{i}-e_{i}>s_{j}+e_{j}\geq q_{j} for every q∈𝒰q\in\mathcal{U}, i∈Si\in S, j∉Sj\notin S. Thus MK​(q)=SM_{K}(q)=S, independently of ties. For two scores outside FrF_{r} with common bound ee, this requires si−sj>2​es_{i}-s_{j}>2e.

Re-ranking. After each round, update SS, boundary scores and margins over the full candidate set. Changes to one score can move unchanged candidates across the boundary; certification uses the updated bounds and comparisons.

Relation to R1+M. With the margins of Appendix I.5, recomputing all compounds at margin below 2​e2e leaves a gap of at least 2​e2e between unrecomputed scores on opposite sides of the original selection boundary. Unrecomputed triage scores remain at least 2​e2e from the threshold. Certification checks the full re-ranked candidate set, including equalities and pairs involving recomputed scores. R1+M used the retrospective maximum residual as ee in one empirical round with ε=2​e\varepsilon=2e. Certified intervals require valid per-score bounds. Row and column checksums locate faulty computations but do not bound individual scores, because errors can cancel within a sum.

The Top-KK condition restates the interval stability criterion in Appendix C.4.

K.3 Observations, history and commitment

For at=π⁡(Ht)a_{t}=\pi(H_{t}), certifying gg fixes the input when every returned field is determined by the certified target; other fields must be certified or omitted. In the experiments with selective recomputation, the hERG agents received the full prediction table after R1+M and reproduced the healthy decisions (Section 5.2); the single-request experiment certified the full table through trusted recomputation (Appendix I.7). Under fixed continuation conditions, restored input determines the endpoint for deterministic agents and its conditional distribution for stochastic agents (Appendix C.4).

Recovery after consumption replaces the affected output in visible history, discards dependent messages, tool records and pending actions, and invalidates server-side state derived from them, including KV-cache entries for discarded tokens or entries computed on untrusted hardware.

Each pending action is bound to its request, computation contract and certificate. In one atomic step, the commit service checks action agreement, certificate currency and uncommitted status, then records commitment; mismatches are rejected. For hERG, it checks the certified selection set or triage vector. Each request commits at most once; exactly-once external execution also requires an idempotent action service keyed by that request. Before commitment, verification failure, budget exhaustion, agent failure and service failure lead to trusted full recomputation or no commitment.

The single-request experiment evaluates verification before the agent reads the scores and after it has used them, with restoration of the execution state and local records of actions accepted under the current certificate (Appendix I.7).
